mcqs.question: What's the key difference between what an example-based test and a property-based test each assert?
options: Property-based tests only work on numeric input, example-based tests work on any type
There is no meaningful difference — both check the same kind of fact
An example-based test asserts a fact about one specific input; a property-based test asserts an invariant meant to hold across a whole generated space of inputs
Property-based tests are always faster to run than example-based tests
mcqs.explanation: Example-based tests specify a single input and its exact expected output, while property-based tests specify a general rule and let a framework generate many inputs to check it against. Property-based testing isn't limited to numeric types, and generating many inputs typically makes it slower per test, not faster.

mcqs.question: A property-based test fails on a randomly generated 200-element list. What does shrinking do to help you debug it?
options: It deletes the failing test so it stops blocking the build
It automatically tries smaller, simpler variations of the failing input and keeps the smallest one that still reproduces the failure
It automatically fixes the underlying bug in the source code
It re-runs the same 200-element input multiple times to confirm the failure is real
mcqs.explanation: Shrinking searches for progressively smaller inputs that still trigger the failure, turning an unwieldy 200-element case into a minimal, human-debuggable repro. It doesn't touch the source code or delete the test, and re-running the same large input wouldn't make it any easier to understand.

mcqs.question: What is fuzz testing primarily designed to find, as distinct from a property-based test's usual goal?
options: Whether a documented business rule was implemented as specified
Whether generated code compiles correctly
Crashes, hangs, or security vulnerabilities triggered by malformed or adversarial input, rather than checking a specific correctness invariant
Whether code coverage exceeds a target percentage
mcqs.explanation: Fuzzing generates inputs specifically to find robustness failures — crashes, hangs, memory-safety bugs — at points where untrusted input reaches code, which is a different goal from property-based testing's focus on verifying a stated correctness invariant. It isn't about business-rule verification, compilation, or coverage percentages.

mcqs.question: A snapshot test captures a component's rendered HTML output once and compares future runs against it. What is fundamentally different about this compared to a normal example-based assertion?
options: Snapshot tests run faster than any other kind of test by design
The stored baseline reflects what the code currently produces, not necessarily what a human verified to be correct — a passing snapshot test proves output didn't change, not that it's right
Snapshot tests can only be used for testing databases
Snapshot tests do not require any stored files at all
mcqs.explanation: A snapshot is captured from the code's actual current output rather than specified by a human deciding what's correct, so a passing snapshot test only proves nothing changed — it says nothing about whether the original captured baseline was ever correct. Snapshot testing applies to many kinds of structured output, isn't inherently faster, and does rely on stored golden files.

mcqs.question: A team has a well-understood business rule with a handful of clear edge cases. Which testing approach fits best for that specific rule?
options: Fuzz testing, since it finds edge cases automatically
Snapshot testing, since it requires the least effort per case
Property-based testing, since it should replace example-based tests wherever possible
Example-based testing — the cases are already known and clearly specified, so hand-writing them is cheap and direct
mcqs.explanation: When the correct behavior and edge cases are already clearly known, hand-writing example-based tests is cheap and directly verifies the intended rule — property-based testing's cost is best spent where an invariant is easier to state than an exhaustive case list, which isn't true here. Fuzzing targets robustness against hostile input, not verifying a known business rule, and snapshot testing is for large output that's impractical to hand-specify.

mcqs.question: A team habitually runs an 'update-snapshots' command whenever a snapshot test fails, without reviewing the specific diff, to unblock CI quickly. What is the long-term consequence?
options: None — snapshot tests are self-correcting over time
The suite runs faster with no loss of signal
The snapshot test suite can stay green for months while silently accepting real regressions, since every failure gets rubber-stamped into the new baseline regardless of correctness
The stored snapshots automatically get smaller and more efficient
mcqs.explanation: Bulk-approving snapshot diffs without review means any regression introduced on the day of a failing run gets baked into the new baseline as if it were correct, so the suite reports green while having quietly stopped verifying anything. This doesn't self-correct, doesn't speed up the suite in any meaningful way, and doesn't shrink the stored snapshots.
